name: Question 3
problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3)+2{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t)=(C{e}^{t/3}-4t-12)f(t)+g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{-t/3}\,\text{d}t=(-3t-9){e}^{-t/3}
$$
worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{-t/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t/3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{3}x{e}^{-t/3} & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{-t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{-t/3}) & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{-t/3} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{-t/3})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4}{3}\int t{e}^{-t/3}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{-t/3} & =\frac{4}{3}(-3t-9){e}^{-t/3}+C \\ x & =-4t-12+C{e}^{t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{t/3}-4t-12.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y=x(t-3)+2{t}^{2},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =(C{e}^{t/3}-4t-12)(t-3)+2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)=t-3,\text{ }g(t)=2{t}^{2},$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t)=2{t}^{2}+t-3.
$$

Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

y=x(dydx−3)+2(dydx)2.

If y′(x)=t, then general solution can be expressed in parametric form (x(t),y(t)), where y(t)=(Cet/3−4t−12)f(t)+g(t) and C is an arbitrary constant. Find f(t)+g(t).

Hint: Under the given transformation, we have dxdt−13x=43t. You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted): ∫te−t/3dt=(−3t−9)e−t/3

EXPLANATION

A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

y=xf(y′)+g(y′), where f and g are differentiable functions of y′.

We're told that, under the substitution y′(x)=t, our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation dxdt−13x=43t.

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

dxdt+P(t)x=Q(t) we compute our integrating factor as follows:

I(t)=e∫P(t)dt=e∫(−13)dt=e−t/3

Multiplying our differential equation by I(t) gives e−t/3dxdt−13xe−t/3=43te−t/3.

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to t, we have

ddt(xe−t/3)=43te−t/3∫ddt(xe−t/3)dt=43∫te−t/3dtxe−t/3=43(−3t−9)e−t/3+Cx=−4t−12+Cet/3.

Therefore, we have that x(t)=Cet/3−4t−12.

To recover y, we substitute x into y=x(t−3)+2t2, which gives

y(t)=(Cet/3−4t−12)(t−3)+2t2.

Finally, we conclude that f(t)=t−3, g(t)=2t2, and f(t)+g(t)=2t2+t−3.
